claim.precise: Psalm 18:2–3 predicted Jesus as the horn of salvation raised in David's house, as Luke 1:69–71 proclaims.
claim.scope_notes: Luke clearly reuses the rare phrase, but Psalm 18 calls the LORD the horn in praise for an experienced deliverance.

context.summary: In Psalm 18 David praises the LORD as rock, fortress and horn of his salvation after rescue from enemies. Zechariah's song says God has raised a horn of salvation in David's house, using the same image for a coming Davidic deliverer.

strongest_case.summary: The distinctive phrase and shared enemy-deliverance setting make scriptural reuse highly likely, whether from Psalm 18 or its parallel in 2 Samuel 22. Luke places the saving strength in David's house and frames it as fulfilment of prophetic promises, presenting Jesus as the agent of God's own salvation.
reasoning: Both passages concern rescue from enemies.
Luke explicitly invokes earlier prophets and David's house.

critical_case.summary: Psalm 18 looks back on deliverance and identifies the LORD himself as the horn; it does not predict a future child or Davidic descendant. Luke transforms a divine-strength metaphor into a title for God's raised deliverer. That is deliberate scriptural development, not direct fulfilment of a forecast in Psalm 18.
reasoning: Luke changes metaphor into a Davidic figure.

verdict.summary: Luke deliberately reuses Psalm 18's horn-of-salvation image for Jesus in David's house. The psalm originally praises God for past rescue, so Luke develops the image rather than reports a stated prediction coming true.

sources.title: Luke's Interpretation of Scripture in Luke 1–2
sources.author: Jonathan Geddes
sources.notes: Identifies the phrase's scriptural source and Lukan use.

objections.objection: Psalm 18 is not proven to be Luke's particular source because Second Samuel 22 is parallel.
objections.reason: The strongest case now names both possible sources.

objections.objection: Changing the grammatical referent does not break continuity in divine action.
objections.reason: The verdict presents Jesus as God's agent rather than a competing referent.

objections.objection: Retrospective rereading can also be theological fulfilment.
objections.reason: The final language distinguishes genre without dismissing fulfilment.

publication_copy.title: The horn of salvation
publication_copy.scripture_excerpt: The LORD is … the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.

website.description: Did Psalm 18 predict Jesus as the horn of salvation?
website.summary: Luke deliberately reuses the image for Jesus, though Psalm 18 originally calls God the horn in praise for past rescue.
website.christian_case: Luke repeats a distinctive phrase, places the saving horn in David's family and says God is fulfilling ancient promises. The connection is strong.
website.critical_case: Psalm 18 calls the LORD himself the horn and celebrates rescue already received. It predicts no future Davidic child. Luke gives the old image a new focus.
website.verdict: Luke's reuse is clear and theologically substantial. It is a retrospective Davidic development of Psalm 18 rather than a direct forecast found there.

carousel.heading: Did Psalm 18 call Jesus salvation’s horn?
carousel.body: David calls God the horn of his salvation. Luke says God raised a horn of salvation in David’s family.

carousel.heading: The phrase is deliberately reused
carousel.body: Both passages celebrate rescue from enemies. Luke presents Jesus as the promised Davidic agent of God’s salvation.

carousel.heading: But the psalm calls God the horn
carousel.body: It praises a rescue already received and predicts no future child. Luke gives the old image a new focus.
